guide.title: Ridgefield, Connecticut: Connecticut's Only Inland Battle
guide.intro: Colonists from Norwalk and Milford founded Ridgefield in 1708, and the town incorporated a year later in Connecticut's southwestern corner on the New York border. It stayed a farming community until wealthy New Yorkers discovered it and began building summer cottages. The Revolution arrived on April 27, 1777: roughly 1,800 British troops under General William Tryon, returning from burning Continental supplies in Danbury, fought Connecticut's only inland battle of the war here. Continental General David Wooster was mortally wounded and died days later in Danbury, while Generals Benedict Arnold and Gold Selleck Silliman organized a barricade of wood and wagons at the north end of town. A British cannonball fired that day still sits lodged in a beam at the Keeler Tavern, a Patriot gathering place. A century later, American Impressionist J. Alden Weir made his home and studio here starting in 1882 — grounds now preserved as Connecticut's first National Historical Park.

sections.heading: The Battle of Ridgefield
sections.body: Ridgefield was founded in 1708 by colonists from Norwalk and Milford and incorporated a year later, and it remained mainly a farming community until wealthy New Yorkers discovered it and built summer cottages within its borders. That changed for one day on April 27, 1777, when roughly 1,800 British troops under General William Tryon, returning from destroying Continental supplies in Danbury, fought the Battle of Ridgefield — Connecticut's only inland battle of the Revolutionary War. Continental General David Wooster was mortally wounded in the fighting and died days later in Danbury, while Brigadier Generals Benedict Arnold and Gold Selleck Silliman organized a makeshift barricade of wood and wagons at the north end of town for the main engagement. A British cannonball fired that day ended up lodged in a beam of the Keeler Tavern, a Patriot gathering place, and can still be seen there today. A century later, Ridgefield's history took a different turn: American Impressionist J. Alden Weir made his home and studio here starting in 1882, on grounds that straddle the Ridgefield-Wilton line and are preserved today as Weir Farm National Historical Park, Connecticut's first National Historical Park.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Ridgefield is a driving town on the US Route 7 / Route 35 corridor: from the north, take I-84 Exit 3 to Route 7 South through Danbury; from the coast, take the Merritt Parkway or I-95 to Route 7 North out of Norwalk; and from New York, take I-287/I-684 to Route 35 East. Metro-North's Danbury Branch of the New Haven Line stops at Branchville station in Ridgefield's Branchville section. Katonah, NY, on the Metro-North Harlem Line, is a common alternative reached by taxi; the nearest Amtrak stops are Stamford, CT (about 22 miles) and New York's Penn Station.

sections.heading: Museums, theaters, and a National Historical Park
sections.body: The Keeler Tavern Museum & History Center interprets colonial-through-early-20th-century Ridgefield on a four-acre Main Street campus, open March through December, Thursday-Sunday. The Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, also on Main Street, is a non-collecting contemporary art museum with a two-acre Sculpture Garden. Weir Farm National Historical Park offers grounds and trails open daily, year-round, with seasonal house tours. The Ridgefield Playhouse presents rock, jazz, comedy, Broadway, classical, and family series, while the Prospector Theater is a first-run nonprofit movie theater whose mission is meaningful employment for people with disabilities.

faq.question: How do I get to Ridgefield?
faq.answer: By car: I-84 Exit 3 to Route 7 South from the north, the Merritt Parkway or I-95 to Route 7 North from the coast, or I-287/I-684 to Route 35 East from New York. By rail, Metro-North's Danbury Branch stops at Branchville station in town; Katonah, NY (Harlem Line) is a common taxi-in alternative, and the nearest Amtrak stops are Stamford and New York's Penn Station.

faq.question: What was the Battle of Ridgefield?
faq.answer: Connecticut's only inland battle of the Revolutionary War, fought April 27, 1777, as roughly 1,800 British troops under General William Tryon returned from burning supplies in Danbury. Continental General David Wooster was mortally wounded and died days later.

faq.question: What is Weir Farm National Historical Park?
faq.answer: The home and studio of American Impressionist J. Alden Weir, who lived there from 1882; it straddles the Ridgefield-Wilton line and is Connecticut's first National Historical Park. Grounds and trails are open daily, year-round.

faq.question: Can I still see the Revolutionary War cannonball?
faq.answer: Yes — a British cannonball fired during the 1777 battle remains lodged in a beam at the Keeler Tavern Museum & History Center on Main Street.

faq.question: Where can I eat and stay in Ridgefield?
faq.answer: Nod Hill Brewery, Luc's Café, and The Hideaway are verified in-town options for food and drink; the West Lane Inn, a 17-room bed & breakfast near the village center, is the town's verified lodging.

places.name: Weir Farm National Historical Park
places.address: 735 Nod Hill Road, Wilton, CT 06897 (the park straddles the Ridgefield-Wilton line; reached via Route 102 from Ridgefield's Branchville section)
places.summary: The home and studio of American Impressionist J. Alden Weir, who lived here from 1882, set on 60-plus acres of woods, fields, and waterways. Grounds and trails open daily, year-round, sunrise to sunset, with seasonal house tours.
places.history: Weir Farm is Connecticut's first National Historical Park, preserving the home and studio of American Impressionist J. Alden Weir from 1882.

places.name: The Ridgefield Playhouse
places.summary: A nonprofit performing arts venue steps from Main Street, presenting rock, jazz, comedy, Broadway, classical, and family series, with free on-site parking.

places.name: Prospector Theater
places.summary: A first-run nonprofit movie theater whose mission is meaningful employment for people with disabilities — about 75% of its staff self-identify with a disability. Also runs a gourmet popcorn shop.

places.name: Nod Hill Brewery
places.summary: A craft brewery with a taproom, biergarten, and live music, pouring hop-forward IPAs, lagers, and traditional cask ales, with rotating food-truck partnerships.

places.name: Luc's Café
places.summary: A French bistro in the heart of downtown Ridgefield, serving continuously Monday-Saturday, 11 a.m.-9:30 p.m.; closed Sundays.

places.name: The Hideaway
places.summary: A local gastropub serving seafood appetizers, Southwestern specialties, and bar classics, with weekend brunch Saturday-Sunday, 11:30 a.m.-3 p.m.; open seven days a week.

places.name: West Lane Inn
places.summary: A 17-room inn near the village center; each room has a private bath, some with working fireplaces or kitchenettes, with complimentary breakfast served on the front porch or breakfast room.
